title: Egocentric Bias
description: Overestimating your own contribution, importance, or visibility relative to others. You think you did more work, your opinion matters more, and others notice you more than they do.
shortDescription: Overestimating your own contribution, importance, or visibility relative to others. You think you did more work, your opinion matters more, and others notice you more than they do.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: Overestimating your own contribution, importance, or visibility relative to others. You think you did more work, your opinion matters more, and others notice you more than they do.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: In a group project, if you ask each member what percentage they contributed, the sum always exceeds 100%.
You remember your comments in a meeting as more insightful than others do.
You think your emotional state is obvious to everyone, while it’s actually invisible.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Over‑sharing personal details assuming high interest.
Feeling under‑appreciated because you see your own effort more clearly than others’ effort.

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “I basically did the whole thing myself.”
“Everyone was staring at me.” (when they weren’t)
“I’m the one who made this happen.”

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: You’re surprised when others don’t know what you’re feeling.
You feel resentment because you think you’re doing more than your share—but you haven’t actually measured.
You assume your perspective is the default.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: We have direct access to our own thoughts, efforts, and emotions; others’ internal states are invisible. This asymmetry creates a natural over‑weighting of the self.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: When assessing contributions, list everyone’s specific tasks and compare objectively.
Ask for feedback: “What percentage of the work do you think I did?” The answer may be jarring but useful.
Assume others are not noticing your internal state unless you communicate it.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Interpreting this bias as proof that others are lazy or ungrateful.
Over‑correcting by downplaying your own contributions, leading to resentment.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A married couple each believes they do 70% of the housework. They argue, certain the other is exaggerating. They log actual time for a week and discover it’s nearly 50/50. Both were genuinely astonished.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: Your effort feels heavier because you’re lifting it. Everyone else’s burden is invisible. Measure, don’t assume.
